name: Dermarolling for hair (microneedling scalp)

card.summary: Rolling or stamping fine needles over the scalp, usually alongside topical minoxidil, to support thicker-looking hair on thinning areas.
card.aka: Scalp dermaroller, scalp microneedling, derma stamp for hair
card.note: Needle devices carry infection risk if shared or unclean; results in trials were small and from short studies.

quick.overview:
Scalp microneedling means using a roller or stamp with fine needles to create tiny punctures in the scalp, typically in the thinning zones. People with androgenetic alopecia use it together with topical minoxidil to try to increase hair density and thickness, which in turn changes how full the hairline and crown look.

The best-known study is a 2013 pilot trial in Indian men with mild to moderate hair loss, where weekly microneedling plus minoxidil produced a larger hair-count increase at 12 weeks than minoxidil alone. A later trial reported a similar direction of effect but described the gain as modest in cosmetic terms.
quick.how: Users describe rolling a device with short needles over the scalp, often at weekly or longer intervals, then applying minoxidil afterwards or at a separate time. Many combine it with finasteride or ketoconazole shampoo, and some also add low-level laser. Results in studies were assessed over about three months or more.
quick.risks: Reported downsides are pinpoint bleeding, redness and soreness, plus infection risk if devices are unclean or shared. Microneedling services combined with blood products have drawn health-department warnings about blood-borne infection. A T Nation poster notes it works as a growth stimulus and does not address androgen-driven miniaturisation.

lead: Dermarolling for hair, also called scalp microneedling, uses a hand roller, pen or stamp covered in fine needles that makes microscopic punctures in the scalp skin. People with thinning hair use it, most often together with topical minoxidil, with the goal of denser and thicker-looking hair at the hairline, temples and crown [1].

The leading clinical evidence is a 2013 randomized, evaluator-blinded pilot study by Dhurat and colleagues in 100 men with androgenetic alopecia, in which weekly microneedling plus twice-daily 5% minoxidil outperformed minoxidil alone over 12 weeks [2]. Microneedling has been described more broadly as a treatment for hair loss that may improve on minoxidil alone, though its overall efficacy remains under study [1].

In forums such as T Nation, posters list dermarolling next to minoxidil, finasteride and low-level laser as options for people worried about hair loss, for instance during testosterone therapy [3][4].

chain: Needles create tiny skin punctures on the scalp
Possible stimulation of the follicles and better minoxidil penetration are proposed mechanisms
More or thicker hair in thinning zones, fuller-looking hairline
angle.text: Users roll or stamp the scalp in thinning areas, usually in combination with minoxidil, to try to raise hair count. Trials measured hair count and patient self-rating after about 12 weeks.

paras: Microneedling, also called dermarolling or skin needling, is a procedure in which fine needles puncture the skin to prompt a repair response. The scalp version is used for hair loss, usually in the thinning zones of androgenetic alopecia, and is often paired with minoxidil [1].

In the 2013 Dhurat pilot study, 100 men with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia were randomised to weekly microneedling plus 5% minoxidil lotion twice daily, or minoxidil alone; 94 completed the 12 weeks. The mean hair count rose by 91.4 in the combination group versus 22.2 with minoxidil alone, and 82% of the combination group reported more than 50% improvement compared with 4.5% of the minoxidil group [2].

A 2018 randomised, single-observer-blinded trial by Kumar and colleagues found the combination also performed better on hair count and satisfaction, although its authors described the response as not cosmetically significant [2]. The Wikipedia article on microneedling cites the 2013 pilot as its sole hair-loss study and says the efficacy of related combined treatments awaits further research [1].

Microneedling is associated with temporary redness and minor bleeding. A New Mexico health department statement on microneedling combined with platelet-rich plasma warned of possible spread of blood-borne infections when equipment is not handled properly [1].

On T Nation, one poster trying low-level laser and dermarolling says the two act as growth agents that do not stop androgen-driven miniaturisation [3]. Another suggests dermarolling together with topical minoxidil and finasteride as a hair-protection stack when considering anabolic steroid use [4].

timeline.event: Dhurat et al. publish a randomized evaluator-blinded pilot of microneedling in androgenetic alopecia [2]
Kumar et al. report a randomized trial of microneedling plus minoxidil [2]

lore.intro: Scalp dermarolling is mentioned in T Nation threads on hair loss during testosterone or steroid use as one of several add-on options [3][4].

claims.claim: Dermarolling plus minoxidil grows more hair than minoxidil alone
claims.believers: Users point to the 2013 study and report adding the roller to a minoxidil routine [4].
claims.experts: The 2013 pilot found larger hair-count gains with the combination at 12 weeks; a 2018 trial agreed in direction but called the effect not cosmetically significant [2].

claims.claim: Dermarolling acts only as a growth agent, not against androgen miniaturisation
claims.believers: A poster states it does not address the underlying androgen sensitivity [3].
claims.experts: Published trials tested it as an add-on to minoxidil rather than to androgen-blocking drugs [2].
